title: ... and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns
who: Campbell R. Harvey, Yan Liu, Heqing Zhu (NBER WP 20592; Review of Financial Studies 2016)
claim: Given the hundreds of factors already tested, a newly discovered factor should clear a t-ratio of about 3.0 rather than the conventional 2.0.
changes: Raise the hurdle in the edges desk from t of 2 to t of 3 and report how many signals were tried before each one shown.

title: The Deflated Sharpe Ratio: Correcting for Selection Bias, Backtest Overfitting and Non-Normality
who: David H. Bailey, Marcos Lopez de Prado (Journal of Portfolio Management 40(5))
claim: Proposes the Deflated Sharpe Ratio, which adjusts a backtest Sharpe for the number of trials run and for non-normal returns (skew and fat tails).
changes: Every sizing-engine backtest since 1940 should print a deflated Sharpe next to the raw one, with the trial count logged.

title: Replicating Anomalies
who: Kewei Hou, Chen Xue, Lu Zhang (NBER WP 23394; Review of Financial Studies 2020)
claim: Of 447 anomalies, 286 (64%) are insignificant at 5% with NYSE breakpoints and value weights, rising to 380 (85%) at a t cutoff of 3.
changes: Test edges with value weights and NYSE breakpoints so microcaps cannot carry a signal.

title: Is There A Replication Crisis In Finance?
who: Theis Ingerslev Jensen, Bryan T. Kelly, Lasse Heje Pedersen (NBER WP 28432; Journal of Finance 2023)
claim: Argues against the replication-crisis view: a Bayesian model finds most factors replicate, cluster into 13 themes, and work out of sample across 93 countries.
changes: Pair the multiple-testing haircut with Bayesian shrinkage by theme rather than throwing out every factor that fails a single t test.

title: Volatility Managed Portfolios
who: Alan Moreira, Tyler Muir (NBER WP 22208; Journal of Finance 2017)
claim: Scaling factor exposure down when recent volatility is high produces large alphas and higher Sharpe ratios across market, value, momentum, profitability and carry factors.
changes: Use as the baseline case for vol-targeting in the sizing engine, read alongside the Cederburg critique.

title: On the performance of volatility-managed portfolios
who: Scott Cederburg, Michael S. O'Doherty, Feifei Wang, Xuemin (Sterling) Yan (Journal of Financial Economics 138(1))
claim: Across 103 equity strategies, volatility-managed versions do not consistently beat unmanaged ones, and realistic out-of-sample versions generally earn lower Sharpe ratios because the spanning regressions are unstable.
changes: Only credit vol-targeting in the engine if it wins in a real-time walk-forward, not in a full-sample spanning regression.

title: A Changing Stock-Bond Correlation: Drivers and Implications
who: Alfie Brixton, Jordan Brooks, Peter Hecht, Antti Ilmanen, Thomas Maloney, Nicholas McQuinn (AQR; Journal of Portfolio Management)
claim: Stock-bond correlation depends on the relative volatility of growth versus inflation news rather than the inflation level, and a simple model explains about 70% of its long-run variation in the US.
changes: Drive the hedge desk's bond-hedge weight off a measured ratio of inflation to growth uncertainty instead of a fixed negative correlation.

title: Pathetic Protection: The Elusive Benefits of Protective Puts
who: Roni Israelov (AQR; Journal of Alternative Investments)
claim: Index puts are less effective at cutting drawdowns than simply holding less equity, and the volatility risk premium can make them raise drawdowns per unit of expected return.
changes: Argues against a put-only tail budget: benchmark the standing tail budget against a plain reduction in gross exposure of equal cost.

title: The Best Strategies for Inflationary Times
who: Henry Neville, Campbell R. Harvey and co-authors (Man Group; SSRN 3813202)
claim: Over 95 years of US, UK and Japan data, unexpected inflation hurts both bonds and equities, while commodities and especially trend-following gave the most reliable protection in inflation surges.
changes: Size the futures trend sleeve as the main inflation-shock hedge and treat long Treasuries as a growth-scare hedge only.
verified: Fetched the Man Group page; SSRN id confirmed via a hosted copy of the PDF.

title: The Rise and Risks of Private Credit (Global Financial Stability Report, Chapter 2)
who: International Monetary Fund
claim: Private credit has never faced a severe downturn at its current size, borrowers are opaque, and managers have incentives to delay recognising losses, so losses could surface suddenly.
changes: Treat reported private-credit marks as lagging and anchor the credit desk on market prices of listed vehicles.
verified: Fetched the IMF chapter 2 executive summary text from imf.org and the GFSR issue page in search.

title: Bank Lending to Private Credit: Size, Characteristics, and Financial Stability Implications
who: Jose Berrospide, Fang Cai, Siddhartha Lewis-Hayre, Filip Zikes (Federal Reserve Board, FEDS Notes)
claim: Argues against an imminent private-credit contagion: bank commitments to private credit vehicles are about $95bn, and a full drawdown stress of about $36bn would cut aggregate bank CET1 by only about 2 basis points, though public BDC leverage rose from about 40% to 53%.
changes: Frame t6 as losses surfacing first in fund NAVs and BDC prices, not as a bank-capital event; watch BDC leverage as the trigger.

title: The Credit Market Lens: What BDC Markets Are Signaling About Private Credit Valuations
who: Lotfi Karoui, with Michael Puempel and Gabriel Cazaubieilh (PIMCO)
claim: BDC equities trade at significant discounts to NAV while the 25th percentile of BDC loan marks (97.51 at March 2026) sits above broadly syndicated loan prices (94.95), and the direct-lending spread pickup over leveraged loans fell from over 300bp to under 100bp.
changes: Add a marks-versus-BSL gap and a BDC price-to-NAV series to the credit desk as the early read on private-credit losses.

title: Risk-Adjusting the Returns to Private Debt Funds
who: Isil Erel, Thomas Flanagan, Michael S. Weisbach (NBER WP 32278)
claim: After adjusting for both equity and debt risk, the typical private debt fund earns a net-of-fee abnormal return statistically indistinguishable from zero; it looks positive only against debt-only benchmarks.
changes: Supports 'not a yield to chase': benchmark any private-credit yield against a blend of equity and loan indices, not a loan index alone.

title: Global Financial Stability Report, April 2026 (Chapter 1: Global Financial Markets Confront the War in the Middle East and Amplification Risks)
who: International Monetary Fund
claim: Hyperscalers are expected to make up 70% of a projected $3.4 trillion of AI capex by 2029 and have raised over $100bn in bonds since January 2025; since 2020 equities and Treasuries have often sold off together, eroding the equity-bond hedge.
changes: Use its useful-life test (a 3-year GPU life cuts aggregate EBIT margin by more than 9 points versus an implied 7 years) as a stress case in the book and filings desks.
verified: Fetched the IMF report text from imf.org.

title: Annual Economic Report 2026, Chapter I: Progress and peril
who: Bank for International Settlements
claim: The five largest hyperscalers are set to spend over $1 trillion on AI capex across 2025 and 2026, outpacing their free cash flow, with circular equity-for-compute deals, poorly disclosed lease-backs, and direct lending funds now holding about 15% of portfolios in AI and IT; it also documents the Hormuz shock that cut crude flows by over 10 mb/d.
changes: Track the share of capex funded by leases and vendor equity stakes as a named t9 indicator, and model a Hormuz-scale oil shock as a standing swan.
verified: Fetched the BIS chapter page on bis.org.

title: Building AI on credit: structures and spillovers (BIS Bulletin 140)
who: Mathias Drehmann, Egemen Eren (Bank for International Settlements)
claim: A growing share of AI capex is funded through long-term debt and off-balance-sheet vehicles whose ratings lean on a few large firms' commitments; spillovers to Treasuries and IG bonds on AI-financing news days in 2026 were small and short-lived.
changes: Read the annex for instrument detail and add an event study of Treasury and IG moves on large AI-financing days to the rates desk.

title: Financial Policy Committee Record, October 2025
who: Bank of England
claim: Equity valuations look stretched for AI-focused tech; the top five S&P 500 firms are close to 30% of the index, the highest share in 50 years, and power or data bottlenecks could trigger a repricing.
changes: Add concentration of the top five names as a book-level risk input alongside single-name limits.
verified: Fetched the Bank of England page.

title: The Simple Macroeconomics of AI
who: Daron Acemoglu (NBER WP 32487)
claim: Argues against large AI macro payoffs: task-level evidence implies no more than a 0.66% TFP gain over 10 years, or under 0.53% after accounting for hard-to-learn tasks.
changes: Keep a low-productivity scenario in the desk's AI cash-flow model so the buildout call is not conditioned on a boom.

title: Generative AI at Work
who: Erik Brynjolfsson, Danielle Li, Lindsey R. Raymond (NBER WP 31161; Quarterly Journal of Economics)
claim: Among 5,179 customer-support agents, an AI assistant raised issues resolved per hour by 14% on average and 34% for novice workers, with little effect on the most skilled.
changes: Use as the micro anchor for an AI-adoption nowcast: watch for gains in junior-heavy, high-volume service functions first.

title: What Investment Data Implies about the AI Transition
who: Jessica Wachter, Jonathan Wachter (NBER WP 35290)
claim: The five largest US tech firms spent $380bn on capex in 2025 with about double forecast for 2026; matching that in a model implies a roughly 2.7x AI-sector productivity boost and extra cumulative GDP growth of 5 to 58 points by 2030.
changes: Gives the constructive side of t1 a model: the same boom raises the risk-free rate about 0.5 points, so the rates desk should expect higher real yields, not lower, if the buildout pays.
verified: Fetched the IDEAS/RePEc listing of the NBER paper.

title: Assessing a Medium-Run Natural Rate of Interest (FRBSF Economic Letter 2026-22)
who: Vasco Curdia (Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco)
claim: Argues against t2: with the funds rate at 3.5-3.75% and inflation about 3%, the real policy rate of roughly 0.5-0.75% sits below a medium-run natural rate of about 1.5%, a somewhat accommodative stance.
changes: Distinguish policy real rates from market long real yields in t2; if tightening is happening it is in term premiums and long TIPS yields, not the policy rate.

title: The Budget and Economic Outlook: 2026 to 2036
who: Congressional Budget Office
claim: Projects a FY2026 deficit of $1.9 trillion (5.8% of GDP) and debt held by the public rising from 101% of GDP in 2026 to 120% in 2036.
changes: Feed the CBO debt path into the rates desk as a structural term-premium driver behind real yields.

title: 2024 United States Data Center Energy Usage Report
who: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory for the US Department of Energy
claim: US data centers used 4.4% of US electricity in 2023 and are projected to use 6.7% to 12% by 2028.
changes: Use the 6.7-12% band as the official range the power names are priced against and flag when utility load filings move outside it.
verified: Fetched the DOE announcement bulletin; the LBNL page itself refused the fetch.

title: Queued Up: 2026 Edition, Characteristics of Power Plants Seeking Transmission Interconnection As of the End of 2025
who: Joseph Rand, Ryan Wiser and co-authors (Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory)
claim: About 1,312 GW of generation and 749 GW of storage sit in US interconnection queues; gas requests rose 86% to 253 GW, median time to operation exceeds 5 years, and only 13% of 2000-2020 requests were built.
changes: Supports power as the binding constraint: track the gas queue and completion rate as leading indicators for firm-power names.

title: Rethinking Load Growth: Assessing the Potential for Integration of Large Flexible Loads in US Power Systems
who: Tyler Norris, Tim Profeta, Dalia Patino-Echeverri, Adam Cowie-Haskell (Duke Nicholas Institute)
claim: Argues against power as a hard limit: the existing US grid could absorb 76 GW of new load at 0.25% average annual curtailment, 98 GW at 0.5% and 126 GW at 1%, with curtailments averaging about 2 hours.
changes: If data centers accept curtailment, the firm-power premium shrinks; the desk should watch for flexible-interconnection deals as a t4 kill signal.
verified: Duke pages blocked the fetch with a bot check; confirmed authors and figures via POWER Magazine's report and the Duke PDF listing in search.

title: LLM inference prices have fallen rapidly but unequally across tasks
who: Ben Cottier, Ben Snodin, David Owen, Tom Adamczewski (Epoch AI)
claim: The price to reach GPT-4-level performance on PhD science questions fell about 40x per year, with declines across milestones ranging from 9x to 900x per year.
changes: Compare token price declines against reported dollar AI revenue growth each quarter to test whether usage outruns deflation.

title: Trends in GPU Price-Performance
who: Marius Hobbhahn, Tamay Besiroglu (Epoch AI)
claim: FLOP/s per dollar doubles about every 2.5 years across 470 GPUs and about every 2.1 years for ML GPUs.
changes: Use hardware deflation of roughly 25-30% a year to sanity check depreciation lives in hyperscaler filings.
verified: Fetched the Epoch AI blog page.

title: AI and Memory Wall
who: Amir Gholami, Zhewei Yao, Sehoon Kim, Coleman Hooper, Michael W. Mahoney, Kurt Keutzer (arXiv 2403.14123; IEEE Micro)
claim: Over 20 years, peak server FLOPS grew about 3.0x every two years versus 1.6x for DRAM bandwidth and 1.4x for interconnect, making memory the main bottleneck for AI serving.
changes: Supports memory as the second bottleneck: weight HBM supply and pricing as a capex driver separate from logic.

title: Memory has grown to nearly two-thirds of AI chip component costs
who: Venkat Somala (Epoch AI)
claim: HBM rose from 52% of AI chip component spending in Q1 2024 to 63% in Q4 2025, with HBM spend growing from about $12bn to $32bn.
changes: Supports memory as the capex inflator: add an HBM cost share series to the nowcast desk.

title: Historical Oil Shocks
who: James D. Hamilton (NBER WP 16790)
claim: Reviews oil shocks from Suez (1956-57) through the 1973-74 embargo, the Iranian revolution, the Iran-Iraq war, the 1990-91 Gulf war and 2007-08, noting most major shocks were followed by downturns.
changes: Calibrate the swans desk's oil scenario to the historical episode set, not a single volatility estimate.

title: World military expenditure 2025 (SIPRI press release and fact sheet)
who: Stockholm International Peace Research Institute
claim: World military spending reached $2,887bn in 2025, up 2.9% in real terms for an 11th straight annual rise, with Europe up 14% to $864bn.
changes: Use SIPRI series as the base for a re-armament budget tracker, with Europe as the growth leg.

title: Guns and growth: The economic consequences of defense buildups (Kiel Report 2)
who: Ethan Ilzetzki (Kiel Institute for the World Economy)
claim: Surveys macroeconomics, public finance and economic history to assess short- and long-run effects of rearmament on output and productivity.
changes: Read for the fiscal multiplier range before assigning a growth or yield effect to European defense budgets.
verified: Fetched the IDEAS/RePEc listing; figures not in the abstract so none quoted.

title: The Golden Dilemma
who: Claude B. Erb, Campbell R. Harvey (NBER WP 18706; Financial Analysts Journal 2013)
claim: Argues against gold as a practical inflation hedge: it hedges over centuries but not over normal investment horizons, and high real gold prices have tended to precede below-average returns.
changes: Keep the gold sleeve small and justify it on debasement and reserve demand, not on inflation hedging.

title: Gold demand: the role of the official sector and geopolitics (box in The international role of the euro, June 2025)
who: Anja Bruggen, Maurizio Michael Habib, Roger Gomis, Alessandro Vallin (European Central Bank)
claim: Central bank gold buying exceeded 20% of global gold demand in 2024 versus about a tenth in the 2010s, and the historical link between gold and real yields broke down after 2022.
changes: Do not model gold as a real-rate trade; drive the sleeve off official-sector demand and sanctions risk.

title: Bitcoin: An inflation hedge but not a safe haven
who: Sangyup Choi, Junhyeok Shin (Finance Research Letters 46)
claim: In a VAR, bitcoin rises after inflation shocks but falls during financial uncertainty shocks, unlike gold, so it is not a safe haven.
changes: Never count the bitcoin sleeve toward the tail budget; it is a debasement position that sells off in crises.
